0.name: No life yet
0.description: The world supports Class {n} life, but the star is too young, or the clock has not run far enough, for it to have started.

1.name: Microbial origin
1.description: The first cells of Class {n} life have appeared. They are microbes.

2.name: Producers
2.description: Class {n} life now makes its own food, and that changes the water and the air.

3.name: Complex cells
3.description: Cells with internal structure have appeared among Class {n} life.

4.name: Multicellular life
4.description: Class {n} life has grown into colonies, mats or bodies big enough to see.

5.name: Animals
5.description: Animals have appeared among Class {n} life.

6.name: Sentient life
6.description: A species of Class {n} life builds tools, settlements and a civilization.

A1.name: Sessile animals
A1.description: Animals that stay where they grow: sponge-like feeders and filter feeders.

A2.name: Small mobile animals
A2.description: Animals that crawl or swim, mostly small, grazing and hunting.

A3.name: Large active animals
A3.description: Big, fast animals. They need a rich supply of oxidant to run on.

1.name: Microbes before light
1.description: Microbes living on chemistry in the water, before any of them learn to use light.

2.name: Oxygenating mats
2.description: Light-eating microbes spread through the sunlit water and begin putting oxygen into it. At first rock and iron soak the oxygen up.

3.name: Protists and plankton
3.description: Cells with internal structure drift in the sunlit water and feed on the mats.

4.name: Plants and sponge-grade life
4.description: Algae and mats cover the shallows, with the first sponge-like feeders among them.

6.name: Sentient life
6.description: A species that builds tools, settlements and a civilization, living on an oxygen-rich world.

1.name: Microbes before light
1.description: Microbes living on chemistry, before any of them learn to use near-infrared light.

2.name: Anoxic mats
2.description: Purple and green mats use near-infrared light and a donor such as hydrogen sulfide or iron. They make no oxygen, and their food web fills the air with methane.

3.name: Complex cells without oxygen
3.description: Cells with internal structure that live without oxygen and feed on the mats.

4.name: Thick layered mats
4.description: Layered mats and colonies. Animals would need an oxidant from some other source.

1.name: Microbes on hydrogen
1.description: Microbes living on hydrogen from rock and water, in vents, deep rock and aquifers.

2.name: Hydrogen-eating communities
2.description: Dark communities that turn hydrogen and carbon dioxide into methane, with no light at all.

1.name: Microbes at the redox edge
1.description: Microbes living where a fuel such as sulfide, iron or ammonium meets an oxidant.

2.name: Chemosynthetic mats
2.description: Mats at vents, seeps and where an oxidant meets sulfide, living on that chemical difference.

3.name: Chemosynthetic protists
3.description: Cells with internal structure that graze the vent and seep mats.

4.name: Chemosynthetic colonies
4.description: Multicellular life around vents and seeps, living on sulfide, iron or ammonium.

5.name: Vent and seep animals
5.description: Animals that live beside the vent and host or eat chemosynthetic microbes: tubeworms, clams and the animals that graze them.

6.name: Sentient life
6.description: A species that builds tools, settlements and a civilization, rising from a chemosynthetic food web.

1.name: Acid-tolerant microbes
1.description: Microbes living in concentrated sulfuric acid, in cloud droplets or pools on warm dry ground.

2.name: Acid plankton and mats
2.description: Plankton in the cloud deck or mats in the pools, living on reduced sulfur and organic carbon, breathing the acid itself.

1.name: Microbes in liquid carbon dioxide
1.description: Microbes living in liquid or supercritical carbon dioxide.

2.name: Dense carbon dioxide communities
2.description: Slow communities that use hydrogen as fuel and shed the water they make.

1.name: Microbes in a hydrocarbon sea
1.description: Microbes living in liquid methane and ethane, at around 90 to 190 K.

2.name: Hydrocarbon sea mats
2.description: Slow mats that live on hydrogen and acetylene and give off methane.

1.name: Microbes in ammonia brine
1.description: Microbes living in cold ammonia-water brine, mostly inside ice.

2.name: Ammonia brine communities
2.description: Slow communities in the brine, living on hydrogen and chemical gradients.

1.name: Silicon microbes in acid
1.description: Microbes whose chemistry includes organosilicon compounds, living in concentrated sulfuric acid.

2.name: Silicon-acid communities
2.description: Mats that leave solid silica behind as they live on reduced sulfur and organic carbon.
